# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: An Updated Narrative Review on Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management

### Introduction and Epidemiology
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a life-threatening form of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction that typically affects women during late pregnancy or in the early postpartum months [1, 2]. The landmark National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) workshop defined PPCM using three strict criteria: development of cardiac failure in the last month of pregnancy or within five months postpartum, absence of an identifiable cause of heart failure, and absence of pre-existing heart disease [3]. A global perspective reveals that the disease burden varies drastically across the world, with highly elevated rates in developing regions and specific ethnic groups [4, 5]. Over the last decade, growing clinical recognition has highlighted PPCM as a critical driver of pregnancy-associated cardiovascular morbidity, maternal mortality, and long-term disability [6, 7]. Large-scale prospective registries, such as those conducted by the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), have provided valuable insights into the clinical course, baseline characteristics, and global management patterns of these patients [8].

### Pathophysiology
Historically regarded as an idiopathic pathology, PPCM is now recognized as a vascular-hormonal disease driven by a "two-hit" mechanism [2]. The central driver is the cleavage of the pituitary hormone prolactin by the protease cathepsin D, yielding a cardiotoxic 16-kDa prolactin fragment [9]. This fragment promotes microvascular endothelial cell apoptosis, impairs cardiomyocyte metabolism, and disrupts capillary networks [9]. Second, late-pregnancy angiogenic imbalance, characterized by high levels of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) secreted by the placenta, neutralizes vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and aggravates myocardial ischemia [10]. Genetic susceptibility also plays an essential role; up to 15% to 20% of PPCM patients carry truncating variants in the titin gene (*TTN*), showing a shared genetic landscape with dilated cardiomyopathy [11, 12]. These genetic variants are thought to pre-dispose women to cardiac failure, which is unmasked by the severe hemodynamic stresses of pregnancy [11].

### Clinical Diagnosis
PPCM typically manifests postpartum, though onset during the late third trimester is possible [13]. Early detection is challenging as typical symptoms—such as fatigue, dyspnea, orthopnea, and peripheral edema—mimic standard physiological changes of late pregnancy [13]. Clinical evaluation must include serial electrocardiograms and cardiac biomarkers, particularly brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) and N-terminal pro-BNP (NT-proBNP) [7, 14]. Confirmatory diagnosis is achieved via transthoracic echocardiography showing a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <45% [1]. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging may be employed to differentiate PPCM from alternative etiologies, such as myocarditis, and to assess myocardial fibrosis [15].

### Management Strategies
The medical management of PPCM requires a collaborative, multidisciplinary cardio-obstetrics team [16]. During pregnancy, standard guideline-directed medical therapies (GDMT), including angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), are strictly contraindicated due to high teratogenic risk [13, 16]. Safe alternatives for gestational management include hydralazine, nitrates, and selective beta-blockers [16]. After delivery, patients should transition to comprehensive GDMT to promote myocardial recovery [16].

Based on the pathophysiology of prolactin-mediated cardiotoxicity, the dopamine-D2 agonist bromocriptine has emerged as a successful disease-specific therapy [17, 18]. Multi-center trials and registries demonstrate that adding bromocriptine to standard heart failure treatment significantly enhances LVEF recovery and clinical outcomes [18, 19, 20]. Since bromocriptine promotes a pro-thrombotic state, its administration requires concomitant prophylactic or therapeutic anticoagulation (e.g., heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin, or aspirin) to prevent thromboembolic events [21, 22]. For patients presenting with severe left ventricular impairment (LVEF <35%) and high risk of sudden cardiac death, a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (WCD) serves as an effective temporary bridge to recovery [23].

### Prognosis and Recurrence
The clinical course and prognosis of PPCM are generally more favorable than other dilated cardiomyopathies [15]. Longitudinal cohorts, such as the Investigations of Pregnancy-Associated Cardiomyopathy (IPAC) study, report that approximately 60% to 70% of patients achieve full myocardial recovery within 12 months, though baseline LVEF <30%, severe left ventricular dilation, and black race are strong predictors of poor recovery [24, 25, 26].

Counseling regarding future pregnancies is of paramount importance [16]. Even in patients with fully recovered left ventricular function, a subsequent pregnancy carries a substantial recurrence risk (20% to 30%), which can lead to rapid clinical deterioration, severe heart failure, or death [27, 28]. If the baseline LVEF has not fully normalized, future pregnancy is strictly contraindicated [7, 27]. Prognosis can also be influenced by other systemic factors, such as thyroid function and subclinical thyroid abnormalities [29]. Finally, managing the holistic needs of PPCM patients is essential, as survivors face significant long-term psychological distress, including high rates of anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder [30].
